content: International reference materials for ferritin have been developed to calibrate laboratory standards for routine assays and to evaluate and standardize new tests for ferritin quantification. The WHO international standard for ferritin, provided by the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control (NIBSC, code 94/572), is commercially available and recommended for use in all assays. Quality controls, including low, medium, and high ferritin concentrations, should be included in every testing run or at least daily. Laboratories conducting ferritin testing for patient care or public health assessments should participate in external quality assurance programs. When measuring ferritin, it is recommended to account for inflammation by concurrently measuring acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP). Inflammation can increase ferritin levels by approximately 30%, leading to a 14% underestimation of iron deficiency. Meta-analyses have shown that both CRP and AGP are necessary to fully estimate the impact of inflammation and to adjust ferritin concentrations accordingly. Adjustments for inflammation can be made by raising the ferritin cut-off values, excluding individuals with elevated CRP or AGP levels, or applying correction factors or regression models. These adjustments should be tailored to the specific conditions of each country or region. Population prevalence thresholds for defining iron deficiency as a public health problem are not yet established using ferritin concentrations. However, quartile values of low ferritin prevalence in children and non-pregnant women may help define the severity of iron deficiency as a public health issue. Further research is needed to validate these approaches and to refine cut-off points for ferritin in various populations, including during pregnancy and in the presence of chronic inflammation or comorbidities. Monitoring and evaluation systems should include equity-oriented indicators to assess the impact of interventions and address health inequities. Dissemination of guidelines and engagement with stakeholders, including policymakers and health workers, is critical for successful implementation and sustainability. High-quality data on iron status are essential for selecting appropriate interventions and monitoring their impact on reducing iron deficiency and anemia.
